intuition: An array of length n cannot contain all n+1 positive values from 1 through n+1, so the answer lies in this small range regardless of how large or negative the input values are. A set would track membership easily, but the constant-space requirement asks us to store that information inside the array itself.

Give each relevant value x a home at index x-1. If the current value belongs somewhere else, swap it into that home and inspect the new value that arrived. Repeating this operation is essential because a single index may expose an entire chain of misplaced values. Out-of-range values carry no useful membership information.

A duplicate needs special care: if its home already contains the same value, swapping makes no progress and would loop forever. Otherwise every swap establishes one correct home permanently. A final scan asks whether position i contains i+1; its first failure is the missing positive. If every home is filled, n+1 is the answer.

A swap cannot displace a correct home: if destination x-1 already contained x, the duplicate guard would prevent that swap. Therefore every executed swap permanently fills one new correct home, even if its displaced value starts another chain.

steps: For nums=[3,4,-1,1], n=4, so only values 1 through 4 need homes.
At i=0, value 3 has home=3-1=2. Swap indices 0 and 2 to get [-1,4,3,1]; -1 is out of range and stops this chain.
At i=1, value 4 has home=3. Swap indices 1 and 3 to get [-1,1,3,4]. Now value 1 has home=0; swapping indices 1 and 0 gives [1,-1,3,4].
The placement phase ends with [1,-1,3,4]. Three and four are already in their correct homes.
The scan accepts index 0 because it contains 1, then fails at index 1. Return 2.

codeNotes.code: while 1 <= nums[i] <= n and nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]:
codeNotes.note: The range check prevents invalid indexing, while the inequality prevents duplicate-value cycles.
Swapping fills a home without losing the displaced value; the surrounding while loop processes that newly exposed value.
After placement, membership is encoded positionally. The first mismatched slot identifies the smallest absent positive, not merely any missing number.
